# The Architecture 2.0 Moonshot {#sec-moonshot}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"The purpose of computing is insight, not numbers."*
>
> — Richard Hamming, *Numerical Methods for Scientists and Engineers* (1962) [@Hamming1962NumericalMethods]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** Richard Hamming, a pioneer in computer science, argued that
computing should yield insight rather than raw data. The distinction matters
here. AI-assisted architecture should help architects ask better questions,
test alternatives, explain mechanisms, and defend decisions. Producing more
candidates is useful only when it improves that work.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
What should computer architecture set as its moonshot for AI-assisted design,
what would a defensible answer have to establish, and what would show that the
bet behind the target has failed?
:::

For roughly fifty years, processor generations improved through a familiar progression where device scaling regularly delivered faster, cheaper, and more energy-efficient transistors. Quantitative analysis gave architects a way to compare the resulting design choices. As scaling slowed, microarchitecture, parallelism, and eventually domain specialization provided the remaining gains [@HennessyPatterson2017QuantitativeApproach; @HennessyPatterson2019GoldenAge]. This shift is visible in fifty years of frontier microprocessor data. Clock frequency plateaued in the mid-2000s and never recovered, while transistor counts continued to rise, core counts turned upward, and frontier power resumed climbing toward 500\ W (@fig-microprocessor-trends).

Clock frequency plateaus in the mid-2000s as Dennard scaling ends, while transistor counts continue to rise, core counts turn upward, and frontier power resumes climbing to 500\ W [@DennardEtAl1974Scaling; @EsmaeilzadehEtAl2011DarkSilicon]. The figure shows frontier values rather than every processor; the era boundaries are approximate [@HennessyPatterson2019GoldenAge].

@fig-microprocessor-trends marks the end of a free lunch [@Sutter2005FreeLunch], exposing the harsh economics of the power/performance wall. Transistor counts kept climbing, but once Dennard scaling ended around 2005, the single-thread gains that had arrived automatically each generation slowed from roughly 50 percent a year to a few percent [@HennessyPatterson2017QuantitativeApproach], and every further gain now had to be bought with power the package could barely dissipate. Dennard scaling ended for a specific physical reason. Supply voltage stopped falling with feature size because threshold voltage had reached the floor set by leakage, and pushing it lower leaves transistors that never fully switch off, so static power climbs sharply. With voltage pinned, each additional transistor clocked at full frequency adds net power, the arithmetic behind both the frequency plateau in @fig-microprocessor-trends and the dark-silicon fraction that followed (the share of the chip that must stay powered off to fit its thermal budget). The field recovered the lost gains first through parallelism and then through specialization. Each turn handed architects more of the machine to manage rather than inheriting it from the next process node. The end of Dennard scaling demands a structural shift, not just faster versions of old tools. The figure's dotted rightmost era marks a prospective next turn. In that prospective era, AI helps architects co-design across those layers rather than tune each in isolation.

The end of Dennard scaling is not the only pressure, and the second one is economic rather than physical. What remains of Moore's law [@Moore1965Cramming] still delivers more transistors at each node, but the cost to design and verify them keeps climbing, and leading-node design has passed the hundreds-of-millions-of-dollars mark (@sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales, @fig-design-cost-composition). Human design effort, not transistor count alone, can now become the binding constraint on what a team can actually ship.

The turn to specialization multiplied the architectures, software interfaces, and physical constraints the architect must hold in view. New dataflows, memory systems, and programming interfaces appeared in quick succession [@HennessyPatterson2019GoldenAge]. Yet much of the coordination among workloads, compilers, simulators, RTL, and physical design still falls directly to architects.

Specialization also made architecture decisions tightly coupled. A new dataflow can simultaneously change memory traffic, compiler mapping, verification effort, and physical feasibility. As these cross-layer dependencies multiply, the resulting design space becomes a massive, rugged, high-dimensional discrete space[^fn-rugged-search-c01] that unaided judgment and exhaustive sweeps cannot cover reliably. In one open benchmarking framework, the DRAM memory controller subproblem alone defines a search space of roughly 19 million configurations, while its accelerator and SoC[^fn-soc-c01] design spaces reach $10^{14}$ to $10^{17}$ [@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym].

Worse, navigating this space carries severe economic stakes. Software errors can be serious, but many can be patched after deployment without remanufacturing the machine. A hardware error that escapes pre-silicon verification and appears only in fabricated silicon can force a respin and add fabrication, validation, and schedule cost. The cost of a mistake forces an architect to coordinate far more models, tools, and evidence just to defend a single choice.

[^fn-rugged-search-c01]: **Rugged search space**: A discrete search space riddled with local optima, where stepwise improvement can strand a search far from the best design. Convexity is not even defined on such a space, so greedy and gradient-style methods carry no optimality guarantee, which is why scale defeats both exhaustive sweeps and human intuition.

[^fn-soc-c01]: **SoC (system-on-chip)**: A single chip that integrates CPU cores, accelerators, memory controllers, and I/O blocks on one die, tied together by an on-chip interconnect. The design space is combinatorial because every block competes with the others for the same power, area, and memory bandwidth, so a local choice rarely stays local.

This pressure does not make AI strictly necessary, but it explains the turn toward AI assistance. The golden age established that specialization is now where the major gains live. The prize has a measured size. Hameed and colleagues found that a general-purpose core spends well over 90 percent of its energy on instruction fetch, decode, and data movement rather than on the arithmetic itself. Stripping that overhead alone buys about an order of magnitude; the rest of the gap they measured comes from what specialization does beyond removing overhead, namely wider parallelism, cheaper data staging, and operations fused into single hardware steps. For the kernels they studied, a fixed-function application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) was roughly 500 times more energy efficient than a general-purpose core [@HameedEtAl2010Inefficiency]. That gap is what specialization chases, and every part of it handed back for programmability is a decision the architect must defend. It also bounds the moonshot, since no search can beat the workload's own overhead structure.

Architecture 2.0 asks whether AI can help architects design those specialized systems under tight cross-layer constraints. Answering that question puts the study that produced an artifact alongside the artifact itself as something an architect designs, because the study is what decides whether the artifact's claims can be believed. The architect remains responsible for the scope and the resulting decision. This chapter states the ambition as a moonshot, introduces the concrete target used throughout the book, and works out what an answer would have to establish before an architect could defend it. A target stated with no way to lose is a slogan rather than a moonshot, so this one also carries the result that would show the bet failed. The chapter distinguishes a candidate from a useful result, progress on a stated part of the challenge from full success, and the quality of the architecture from the contribution made by AI.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Frame a system-and-chip moonshot with fixed conditions, study-specific choices, and a result that would show its enabling assumption failed.
- Translate a compact system request into its workload, software, hardware, physical, and result requirements.
- Distinguish a candidate from a useful result, progress on a stated part of the challenge from full success, and an architecture outcome from AI contribution against a credible conventional process.
- Use Amdahl's law, the roofline, and a scoped efficiency claim to challenge a design before spending simulator or EDA time.
- Explain how AI participation changes architecture work and judge current systems by the scope, cost, and support behind their results.

:::

## The AI-Assisted Proposition

The field is now applying AI to the design processes that produced those accelerators, targeting tasks from design-space exploration to physical placement [@WangEtAl2026AgentDSE; @MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement]. In this book, *AI* serves as an umbrella term. It includes learned methods for prediction, generation, optimization, and other task-specific uses, as well as systems that combine those methods with conventional analysis and design tools.

Applying these methods to architecture runs into two immediate limits. Much of
the high-fidelity hardware data stays proprietary, and model use adds
computational overhead, latency, and financial cost. Any claimed benefit must
therefore account for both the simulator or engineering work saved and the work
needed to check that a generated claim holds for the physical design.

These limits become concrete when a short product request expands into work
across the full design stack. Consider the following design brief.

> **Lighthouse prompt.** Design a low-power, 64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem for an
> XRBench-class real-time mobile XR workload. Realize it as a vector-capable CPU, accelerator, or SoC block under a 3\ W TDP target in a 3\ nm-class LP mobile process, and return a design-space report with evidence and rejected alternatives.

We call this the *Lighthouse prompt*. Here XR means extended reality, TDP means
thermal design power, and LP identifies a low-power process. XRBench is a public
suite of mobile XR workloads rather than a complete product specification
[@KwonEtAl2023XRBench]. Among the public systems reviewed for this edition, none
establishes an end-to-end answer. The prompt's scale deliberately exposes
the architecture work that a smaller generation task would hide, providing a
long-term target for judging progress toward the full challenge. The prompt targets mobile XR
specifically because it forces simultaneous extreme constraints on latency,
thermal limits, and energy efficiency. It also forces cross-layer integration. An
accelerator block in an industrial SoC is not a clean-sheet island; it must
interface with legacy, black-box IP over rigid standard protocols (like AMBA
AXI)[^fn-axi-c01]. A proposed design is dead on arrival if it optimizes power,
performance, and area (PPA) but drops an AXI handshake.

[^fn-axi-c01]: **AMBA AXI**: The ARM-defined on-chip bus protocol most SoC blocks use to talk to one another. Its handshake is a strict per-channel valid and ready contract, so a block that violates the protocol cannot be dropped into an existing chip no matter how good its power and performance numbers look in isolation.

This compact prompt is not yet enough to guide real architecture work. The architect must still define the workload and reference design, choose meaningful alternatives, connect them to executable tools, and decide what evidence could support or overturn a recommendation. While AI may assist with each step, it can also propose candidate designs, scripts, and summaries far faster than the architect can evaluate them.

The prompt does not imply a single model or invocation. Answering it takes an XRBench trace, a compiler that can target whatever the proposal invents, a simulator, a synthesis run against a low-power library, and a reviewer who can say which of those results the recommendation actually rests on. What this book studies is that whole assembly and the decision it supports, not the fluency of any single generated response.

Two words in those sentences, *AI* and *agent*, carry weight for the rest of the book, so it is worth fixing them now rather than letting each chapter mean something slightly different.

> **AI** names a field and a set of techniques, not one monolithic component.
> An AI method belongs to a family such as generation, prediction, or
> optimization. Its role names the job it performs in the design work. Common
> roles include proposing candidates, estimating consequences, choosing what
> to try next, challenging assumptions, repairing artifacts, and checking
> stated properties. One method can serve more than one role, and a role may be
> filled by a learned method, a conventional tool, or an architect. A role
> describes the work, not the authority of its output. A declared check still
> establishes only what its assumptions, fidelity, and independence support.

> An **agent** is narrower still. It is a software entity that takes actions in an environment, reads what comes back, and decides its next action from that feedback, in a loop, without a person in between each step. A model that answers one prompt is not an agent. A script that runs a fixed sequence of tools is not an agent either, because nothing in it changes course on what the tools returned. The word is used in this book only where all three hold, and where an argument turns on which role is acting rather than on autonomy, the role name is used instead.

If a method proposes a thousand accelerators but a reviewer cannot test why they differ, explain why most should be rejected, or state what would overturn the apparent winner, the extra proposals have not advanced the design. A fast analytical model could still help by screening out thermal-budget violations before they consume scarce simulator or physical-design time. But the value lies in reducing expensive engineering work, not in the raw proposal count.

We use this same Lighthouse prompt throughout the book. Later chapters focus on
different parts of the work without quietly changing the challenge or what a
useful answer must establish.

## A Short History of AI in Architecture

Pursuing this prompt builds on a deep existing foundation. AI has a long history inside computer architecture, where researchers have applied it to branch predictors, prefetchers, surrogate models, reinforcement-learning[^fn-reinforcement-learning-c01] controllers, design-space exploration, and autotuning. Chen, Penney, and Jiménez survey this progress in *AI for Computer Architecture: Principles, Practice, and Prospects* [@ChenPenneyJimenez2020AIArchitecture]. Their synthesis organizes established and emerging AI techniques and applications across computer architecture. This book uses the complete system-and-chip design study as its unit of analysis. It asks how architects decide whether to use AI, assign methods to roles, connect them to existing software and EDA tools, compare the complete approach with a credible alternative at comparable total cost, and remain responsible for the resulting action. Predictive design-space exploration and tensor-program autotuning offer early examples of this integration [@IpekEtAl2006PredictiveDSE; @ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM]. In most of this prior work, learning operates either inside an artifact or performs a specific tactical job within a human-defined architecture workflow. @sec-appendix-b-ai-for-architecture-map groups this prior work into families and maps each to the chapters that develop it.

[^fn-reinforcement-learning-c01]: **Reinforcement learning (RL)**: A machine-learning method in which an agent learns to choose actions that maximize a cumulative reward signal from its environment [@SuttonBarto2018ReinforcementLearning]. In an architecture study it is one search method among several, and its proposals need the same evidence and checks as any other candidate generator.

Recent generative systems are now tackling specific parts of that workflow, such as proposing architecture configurations, invoking tools, and revising searches based on returned results [@WangEtAl2026AgentDSE; @HeEtAl2024ChatEDA]. Domain-adapted language models like ChipNeMo, tuned on internal design data for chip-design assistant tasks, are a concrete instance of this trend [@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo]. While these systems can generate text and scripts, those artifacts represent only a fraction of the effort required to connect an architecture question to a final decision. This book's scope includes both learned components embedded within a design and AI systems used to conduct the broader engineering work. In either context, the central question is how the method changes the evidence supporting an architectural conclusion.

Architecture work has always moved through repeated cycles of analysis and revision. The architect frames a problem, chooses abstractions, constructs models, selects workloads, explores alternatives, evaluates results, rejects weak candidates, and revises the underlying assumptions. This progression moves from intent and workload characterization to architecture decomposition, construction, evaluation, explanation, and finally decision.

Consider weighing a larger L2 cache for a stated workload mix. An architect might use gem5, a cycle-level architectural simulator, or FireSim, an FPGA-accelerated full-system RTL platform, to sweep cache sizes across representative workloads [@BinkertEtAl2011Gem5; @KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]. The architect compares miss behavior, execution time, and energy estimates before explaining whether locality, contention, or latency hiding drove the outcome. Throughout this process, simulators, compilers, synthesis tools, and design reviews mediate the architect's judgment of whether the evidence justifies a design change.

The method family and the architecture job are related but not identical.
Generation can propose a new artifact or repair one after a failed check.
Prediction can screen candidates or estimate a consequence that has not yet
been measured. Optimization can decide where to spend a limited evaluation
budget. Critique and verification are different jobs that may use conventional
or learned methods. These jobs need not occur in a fixed order, and a repair
that changes the artifact may invalidate earlier measurements.

The distinction becomes concrete in the Lighthouse study. Trying to integrate a
generated accelerator can expose a missing compiler or interface constraint
when no legal software path can use the candidate. A predictor may show that
its uncertainty is too large to separate two cache candidates. An optimizer may
allocate the next scarce simulator or EDA run, while critique or verification
may disqualify an apparent winner that violates an interface, timing, or
thermal condition. Generation, prediction, and optimization therefore earn
their place through the engineering work they remove and the checks their
outputs still require.

To evaluate any of these AI contributions, an architect must be able to identify the work assigned to each method, the information and tools it used, what it changed, the cost it incurred, and which measurements support the resulting conclusion.

Architecture practice already combines human judgment with simulators, compilers, EDA optimization, scripts, generators, and extensive automation. Learned methods may change the balance of work when they can propose or screen more alternatives, interpret less structured information, or coordinate work across tools. The architect then spends more time specifying the problem, deciding what work to delegate, checking whether an objective omits a constraint, and interpreting the resulting tradeoffs. An optimizer told to minimize power may share hardware resources that were isolated for a reason, reintroducing microarchitectural contention channels such as shared-cache timing leaks or simultaneous multithreading (SMT) port contention, because nothing in the objective priced them. The degree of AI participation can vary, and assigning a method more work never transfers responsibility for the final architectural conclusion.

While embedded ML optimizes run-time behavior by living inside the artifact, the chapters ahead focus on AI methods used in design work itself. AI-assisted architecture extends a long history of design automation, but it begins from a broader statement of intent than earlier tools. It is not defined by automating more steps.

Five developments illustrate how design automation can accept different levels
of intent and produce different artifacts. The dates are approximate, the
developments overlap, and AI-assisted architecture remains a research
direction rather than an inevitable next step.

1. **1980s--1990s (Logic Synthesis):** Logic synthesis translated Boolean and RTL descriptions into gate-level structure under library, physical, and timing constraints [@DeMicheli1994SynthesisOptimization].
2. **1990s--2000s (High-Level Synthesis):** High-level synthesis, with behavioral-synthesis roots in 1980s research and commercial adoption reaching into the 2010s, generated RTL candidates from algorithmic descriptions and moved part of the tactical microarchitecture search into tools [@CoussyMorawiec2008HighLevelSynthesis].
3. **2000s--2010s (Domain-Specific Synthesis):** Building on deductive program synthesis from the 1970s, domain-specific synthesis generated executable code from specifications constrained by domain-specific languages [@GulwaniPolozovSingh2017ProgramSynthesis].
4. **2010s--2020s (Agile Hardware Generation):** Agile hardware generation used parameterized templates, such as Chisel and its FIRRTL intermediate representation, to create specialized SoC instances from reusable IP [@chipyard].
5. **Prospective direction (AI-Assisted Architecture):** AI may help connect workload intent, software contracts, architectural alternatives, executable tools, experiments, and physical constraints inside a scoped study. The research question is whether the result can become a finding or decision supported by evidence, even when much of the study remains under human control.

These earlier developments remain essential. Logic synthesis became practical at scale in part because static timing analysis and equivalence checking could reliably expose bad netlists. AI-assisted architecture draws on these established tools while connecting decisions made across stages. The evidence must identify which tool produced each result and which assumptions limit how that result can be used.

Reviewable evidence from iterative work should include the proposals
considered, the results obtained, the candidates rejected or revised, and the
decisions that followed. Different readers use this information for different
reasons.

- **Researcher:** Describe an AI-for-architecture paper by naming the
  architecture question, the role AI played, the artifact or finding produced,
  and the evidence and limits behind it.
- **Tool builder:** Ask whether a harness keeps the inputs, settings,
  results, and failures that another method or engineer would need.
- **Author or reviewer:** Ask what would reject the claim, why the measured
  mechanism supports it, and which decision it can justify.

## Transitioning from Architecture 1.0 to 2.0 {#sec-from-architecture-10-to-architecture-20}

These review questions apply whether the architect directs every step or AI participates in part of the work. Architecture 1.0 is shorthand for familiar, human-directed practice, which already includes analytical models, scripted flows, automated search, parameterized generators, and EDA optimization. Architecture 2.0 retains that foundation and responsibility while allowing learned methods to perform selected roles across more of the work [@ReddiYazdanbakhsh2025Architecture20]. The distinction concerns the breadth and role of AI participation, not manual work versus automation, as summarized in @tbl-arch1-vs-arch2.

| **Feature** | **Architecture 1.0** | **Architecture 2.0** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Problem framing | Architects define the question, abstractions, constraints, and tool tasks | Learned methods may help translate broader intent or incomplete information into proposed study choices that the architect reviews |
| Exploration | Architects use analytical models, scripts, parameterized generators, sweeps, and classical optimization | Prediction, generation, and learned optimization may propose, screen, or select alternatives alongside conventional methods |
| Tool use | Architects and scripts invoke simulators and EDA tools, preserve results, and decide what to run next | Automated components may select later actions from tool returns, so state, cost, failures, and permitted actions must be available to the component and reviewer |
| Decision making | Architects integrate results and remain responsible for the design decision | Methods may organize analysis or prepare a recommendation, while architects retain responsibility for the design decision |

: **AI participation broadens what may be delegated without changing who owns the decision:** Architecture 2.0 adds learned prediction, generation, optimization, or tool coordination to established analytical and automated practice while the architect retains scope and judgment. {#tbl-arch1-vs-arch2}

The comparison is not manual work versus automated work. It identifies where learned methods may act and what the architect must still specify and judge. Independent checking is one requirement, not the whole distinction. Logic synthesis provides the precedent. Static timing analysis and equivalence checking made automated netlist generation practical because they could expose timing and functional failures before signoff. The same principle applies to learned methods, but the relevant check depends on the assigned job. A generated design needs legality and implementation checks, a prediction needs calibration against higher-fidelity results, and an optimization result needs a comparison that accounts for the objective and omitted constraints.

AI may help the architect interpret an initial request, characterize workload
distributions, propose an architecture decomposition, construct artifacts,
select evaluations, diagnose results, and prepare a recommendation. These are
possible forms of assistance across several methods, not a claim that any
single public system performs the complete workflow today. Producing a
plausible artifact does not replace intent framing, workload
characterization, evaluation, or decision making.

When AI takes on more of this work, another architect still needs enough
information to reconstruct what happened and determine exactly what the result
supports.

During the XR subsystem exploration, for example, a method might propose vector-lane configurations, a surrogate[^fn-surrogate-model-c01] could screen them for 3\ W thermal violations, and a critic could flag unsupported compiler intrinsics. The architecture work may end in a novel cache design, an architectural finding, a reusable method, or a decision supported by the available evidence.

[^fn-surrogate-model-c01]: **Surrogate model**: A cheap, data-driven stand-in for an expensive simulator that lets a method screen many candidates quickly. Its score is only a proxy, so a promising candidate still needs a higher-fidelity check before it can support a design decision.

Whatever the output, the architecture outcome and the contribution made by AI
are separate judgments. The architecture outcome states what the comparison
supports about the subsystem, including rejection or no change. The AI
contribution states what the assistance changed relative to a competent
conventional process, including the result quality, work completed, information
obtained, and total cost. A good design does not prove that AI improved the
work, and a faster study does not prove that the design is better.

@fig-design-loop-breaks illustrates one practical requirement of AI participation. Conventional studies can and often do record their inputs, artifact versions, tool results, rejected candidates, and decisions. When an automated component chooses actions from that information, the relevant state must also be represented in a form the component can use and a reviewer can inspect.

![**AI participation requires usable design state.** Both studies can record inputs, actions, tool results, rejected candidates, and decisions. When automated components act on that information, it must also be represented where the components can use it and reviewers can inspect it.](images/F2a-design-loop-breaks){#fig-design-loop-breaks width="85%" fig-alt="Two side-by-side diagrams compare human-orchestrated and AI-assisted architecture studies. Both preserve design state and depend on architectural judgment. AI participation additionally requires the relevant inputs, actions, tool results, and decision responsibility to be usable by automated components and inspectable by reviewers."}

Read the left panel as a familiar human-orchestrated study. Intent moves through
models and scripts to a candidate, tool feedback, and expert review, while much
of the state, rationale, and history remains in expert practice. On the right,
follow the blue path from representation through the environment and methods to
evidence. Weak evidence returns through reject or revise to update the
represented state. The two inward arrows reserve acceptance, revision,
escalation, and commitment for architect review. Making this state explicit
does not make the result correct. It makes the inputs, actions, failures, and
decision authority available for checking.

An AI system that calls a simulator, writes RTL, or summarizes papers still depends on sound systems engineering. Machine learning has long grappled with the sim-to-real gap, where success in simulation does not transfer to the physical setting [@TobinEtAl2017DomainRandomization]. Hardware design has a related fidelity problem. A fast surrogate for congestion or timing can rank candidates differently from the EDA tools used for signoff. Functional simulation, emulation, synthesis, place and route, and physical checks expose different properties at different costs. A method may therefore select a candidate using an inexpensive estimate and later see that candidate fail when the study reaches a more faithful tool.

A generator might propose a mathematically elegant instruction extension that passes behavioral simulation as valid text, only to fail Logic Equivalence Checking (LEC), violate DRC rules, miss PPA targets, or create a large thermal hotspot in the physical silicon. The architect must identify these physical limits, account for memory movement, compare tradeoffs numerically, and decide what evidence justifies moving the generated candidate out of simulation and into the physical design flow.

An AI-assisted study should present a concise rationale connecting its proposals, tool results, and rejected alternatives to its final recommendation. This rationale is not evidence by itself, as @sec-feedback-verification-trust details the criteria making an observation relevant to a claim under stated conditions. Instead, a rationale gives the reviewer a structured account to inspect for missing assumptions, contradictions, or conclusions unsupported by the measurements.

Safety engineering offers a useful precedent. Later decisions are checked against the assumptions, hazards, and evidence on which they originally depended [@Leveson2012EngineeringSaferWorld]. If a subsequent workload shift changes the locality behavior, the architect can trace the rationale to see exactly why the earlier conclusion may no longer apply.

None of this scales by reading faster. A generator that emits thousands of plausible candidates a day defeats per-candidate review. The architect must instead inspect the intended design space, permitted changes, selection method, checks, retained measurements, and representative accepted and rejected candidates. The harness should record the inputs, results, failures, and decisions as the work runs, because manual record keeping does not scale with proposal volume. This makes the study and the scope of its conclusion reviewable without pretending that an architect examined every candidate.

While these practices make individual projects easier to review, the larger question is whether they can support AI across a much greater share of architecture design. Achieving that structural shift requires a target beyond incremental tool upgrades.

## The Lighthouse Prompt and the Architecture Moonshot {#sec-intent-vs-spec}

Engineers use the term *moonshot* for an ambitious goal requiring more than incremental improvement. X, the Moonshot Factory, describes a moonshot as the intersection of a massive problem, a radical solution, and a technological breakthrough making progress plausible [@XCompanyMoonshotBlueprint]. We now state the Lighthouse prompt as an architecture moonshot that spans the entire stack.

![**A compact prompt hides a full architecture study.** The prompt implies architecture requirements and engineering work that must be completed before an architect can turn it into a supported result and decision.](images/F1-moonshot-stack){#fig-moonshot-prompt width="85%" fig-alt="Stacked diagram with the full Lighthouse prompt at the top, architecture requirements in the middle, and the execution and analysis requirements needed to support an answer at the bottom."}

Read @fig-moonshot-prompt from top to bottom. The compact prompt names the
workload, ISA basis, compute alternatives, power and process envelope, and
requested report. The middle layer expands those phrases into workload,
software, hardware, memory, physical, reliability, and verification
requirements. The lower layer turns those requirements into represented study
state, methods and tools, evidence, and decision support. Architect
judgment can redirect the study at each layer. The figure therefore describes
the hidden work behind the prompt, not a prompt-to-chip automation pipeline.

While the full solution to the moonshot may remain distant, the target must be specific enough to organize the field's experiments and highlight which advances actually matter.

Computer architecture has comparable precedents. The Mead and Conway VLSI methodology[^fn-vlsi-complexity-c01] joined abstractions and design rules to tools, fabrication access, and pedagogy [@MeadConway1980VLSI]. The reduced-instruction-set program later reshaped the hardware and software contract around quantitative evidence [@PattersonDitzel1980RISC]. Because both efforts produced new methods and sharable artifacts rather than single designs, other groups could build on and teach them rather than starting from scratch.

[^fn-vlsi-complexity-c01]: **VLSI complexity (origin)**: Early-1980s frontier microprocessors held about $10^4$ to $10^5$ transistors, and by 2021 frontier chips held tens of billions [@Rupp2022MicroprocessorTrendData]. Mead and Conway answered that outgrowth of transistor-level practice with higher-level abstractions, design rules, and fabrication access that a course could teach and a community could share.

> **Architecture moonshot.** An architecture moonshot is a difficult,
> long-term target that existing tools and design practice cannot yet
> address end to end. It seeks a major improvement in how architects
> use AI to turn system and chip design questions into supported results and
> decisions. Advances in AI, data, or tools must make at least part of the
> target practical to investigate without implying that the whole problem has
> been solved.

An architecture moonshot needs all three conditions at once, combining a grand
challenge, a radical practice target, and an enabling breakthrough
(@fig-moonshot-venn). The grand challenge represents complex architecture work
that current ad hoc coordination cannot handle effectively. The radical target
envisions a rigorous practice that uses AI across more of system and chip
design. The enabling breakthrough is the convergence of AI, data, and tools
making part of that target practical to investigate today. Because none of the
three conditions is sufficient alone, their intersection identifies a problem
worth solving, a novel approach, and a practical starting point for testing,
even if the complete goal remains out of reach.

![**The moonshot sits where all three conditions meet:** it combines a major architecture challenge, a substantial change in AI-assisted design work, and an advance in AI, data, or tools that makes part of the problem practical to study.](images/F1c-moonshot-venn){#fig-moonshot-venn width="85%" fig-alt="Three-circle Venn diagram showing an architecture moonshot at the intersection of a grand challenge, a radical practice target, and an enabling breakthrough."}


```{=latex}
\FloatBarrier
```

The three conditions do not carry equal risk. An architect can state a grand challenge and a radical target at the outset, but the enabling breakthrough is a claim about capability that has to hold in practice. A program that assumes that breakthrough rather than demonstrating it, and that names no result that would show the assumption wrong, can pursue the target for years on a premise that never arrives.

::: {.callout-war-story title="The compiler breakthrough EPIC assumed never arrived"}
**The claim.** In the 1990s, Intel and HP bet a processor generation on Explicitly Parallel Instruction Computing (EPIC), the architecture behind Itanium. EPIC moved the work of scheduling instructions from the hardware to the compiler, exposing parallelism at compile time and promising a step-change in performance over the out-of-order designs of the day [@SchlanskerRau2000EPIC].

**The gap.** That payoff depended on a sufficiently smart compiler able to find and schedule the parallelism statically. For behavior known only at run time, such as memory latency and branch outcomes, that compiler never arrived. Out-of-order superscalar processors and the AMD64 extension, announced in 1999, specified in 2000, and shipping around 2003, delivered the gains on existing software instead, and the first Itanium silicon reached the market as Merced only in 2001 [@AMD64History].

**The lesson.** A moonshot's three conditions are not equally safe to assume. Itanium's outcome had several technical and market causes, but EPIC still illustrates the risk of depending on a capability whose limits become clear only after large commitments. A program needs an early result that can challenge its enabling assumption. Current AI-assisted architecture carries a similar risk if it assumes that language models can generate physically realizable microarchitectures without adequate design knowledge, represented constraints, and tool-based checks. Tools can expose violations, but repeated rejection alone does not show that a method can produce a working design.
:::

The Lighthouse prompt, asking for a low-power 64-bit RISC-V compute subsystem for mobile XR, fits all three conditions. Today, architects coordinate decisions across workloads, software, hardware, tools, and physical design. The long-term aim is for AI to take on more of that search, while the architect stays answerable for the claim. Advances in models, data, and tools make configuration search and placement practical to study now.

Tool-using design-space agents already propose configurations, invoke
simulators, and revise searches from returned results, while learning-based
placement can turn a netlist into a macro layout. Each makes one specific design
task practical to study rather than solving the whole problem. The
enabling breakthrough is therefore the condition most easily assumed rather
than demonstrated.

The Lighthouse target carries two tests. Full architectural success requires a
supported design that meets the fixed Lighthouse conditions and the complete
design-space report promised by the prompt, with a recommendation an independent
architect can examine. Demonstrated AI contribution requires a comparison with
the strongest practical conventional or human-directed process for the same
question, starting information, tool access, budget, and stopping rules. AI has
added value only if it improves the architecture result, lowers the total cost
of reaching a result of comparable quality, or both. It has failed within the
assessed program if it improves neither.

This chapter cannot settle either test. Random search can provide a useful
floor, but it is not the credible conventional comparison. A program verdict
also needs repeated comparisons that account for the search, tool, verification,
review, and engineering costs rather than scoring the final artifact alone.
@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect develops those comparisons. The public
evidence reviewed for this edition does not yet return a program verdict.

A target stated this way needs *architecture* and *architect* defined, since the stop condition turns on who owns the claim and on how much of a system the target covers. Architecture is more than a microarchitecture, block diagram, or chip artifact.

> **Architecture.** Architecture is the hardware and software contract and system organization turning workload intent and technology constraints into a defensible system design. It includes the instruction set architecture (ISA), microarchitecture, memory, interconnects, accelerators, chiplets, compiler interfaces, physical-design constraints, verification plans, deployment models, and the evidence used to justify choices.

> **Architect.** The architect is the owner of the decision. The architect frames the problem, chooses abstractions, sets the evidence standard, defines what disqualifies a candidate, and remains answerable for the committed design. While one person may hold this role or a team may divide the work, the division must explicitly state who holds decision and approval authority. Methods can contribute candidates and analysis, but the architect remains responsible for synthesizing the results into a recommendation and defending the ultimate architectural claim.

These definitions set the scope of the Lighthouse answer. It must cover the
hardware and software system, and an architect must be able to defend the
resulting recommendation.

## Unpacking Lighthouse Architecture Questions {#sec-why-the-prompt-spans-the-stack}

The prompt occupies only a few lines, but answering it requires choices about the workload, software contract, compute organization, memory, power, compiler, runtime, physical design, reliability, and verification (@fig-moonshot-prompt). The bottom panel of the figure shows the work required to connect those choices to tools, evidence, and an architectural decision.

```{=latex}
\FloatBarrier
```

Start with the prompt itself. High-level intent first becomes questions and coupled design choices, not a generated chip artifact. The prompt tasks the architect with comparing several compute organizations for a real-time mobile XR workload, all while respecting a 3\ W TDP[^fn-tdp-c01] budget and the limits of an LP process. Individual phrases bound different parts of the study.

[^fn-tdp-c01]: **TDP (thermal design power)**: The sustained power a part is expected to dissipate and the cooling solution is designed to remove, rather than a peak instantaneous draw. A headset has no fan, so the 3\ W figure is really a statement about how much heat the enclosure can shed before its surface becomes too hot to wear.

The phrase "64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem" fixes the word length and
ISA family. Each study must still choose the exact ISA extensions,
ABI[^fn-abi-c01], compiler, runtime, and software contract. The "XRBench-class
real-time mobile XR workload" specification sets the target environment. The
"accelerator block" provision leaves several compute organizations open for
comparison. Finally, the 3\ W target and 3\ nm-class LP process supply hard
physical limits that can rule out an unfeasible proposal. A 3\ W TDP in a
mobile XR form factor forces passive cooling, strict skin-temperature limits,
dense advanced packaging, and high-bandwidth signaling under a tight power
budget.

[^fn-abi-c01]: **ABI (application binary interface)**: The binary-level agreement on register usage, calling conventions, stack layout, and data alignment that lets separately compiled code interoperate. Adding a custom instruction changes the ISA, but shipping it means the compiler, libraries, and operating system have to agree on the ABI as well, which is why an ISA extension is a software project rather than a hardware edit.

While the prompt asks for a design-space report, the study may also produce software, models, RTL, layouts, prototypes, or a physical chip, depending on the ambition of the claim. The report connects those artifacts and measurements to the proposed design and explains precisely why alternatives were rejected. To test the architect's judgment, the prompt deliberately leaves the accelerator microarchitecture, memory system, software integration, and evaluation tools open.

Turning those choices into a study requires formal constraints. Requirement translation already combines profiling, analytical models, prior designs, design tools, and expert judgment. A product request such as "we need a low-power AR headset" does not determine a 3\ W TDP, a particular RISC-V extension, or an L2 capacity on its own. The architect must derive those study parameters from workload and system evidence.

Learned methods can assist by extracting candidate constraints from requirement documents, relating them to prior designs and public benchmarks, and identifying ambiguities for the architect to resolve. When a prompt asks for a "real-time" workload, a language model might ask whether that means a strict 11 millisecond frame deadline at 90\ Hz, a 20 millisecond motion-to-photon bound, or a 99th-percentile tail-latency target.

This assistance does not remove the architect's formulation work. It may reduce the time spent assembling candidate specifications, while the architect still decides whether the proposed bounds are complete and supported. Before search begins, the accepted constraints should be represented in a form the relevant tools can use, such as a parameterized generator configuration or a sweep specification. Prose alone cannot define the legal design space.

Each fragment of the Lighthouse prompt implies a cluster of architectural
decisions and the checks that could disqualify an answer
(@tbl-moonshot-decomposition). AI may
suggest a hardware and software decomposition. The architect accepts, revises,
or rejects that proposed scope and its coupled interfaces.

| **Prompt fragment** | **Architectural decisions** | **What must be checked** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **XRBench mobile XR** | Workload slice, input distribution, quality-of-service target, latency deadline, memory traffic, software pipeline, and drift assumptions. | Trace source, benchmark version, documented workload-phase selection, and rejection when results over-optimize a single hot loop or miss real-time behavior. |
| **64-bit RISC-V with vector or accelerator option** | ISA boundary, custom extension policy, programming model, compiler/runtime path, library support, and software compatibility. | Correctness, toolchain support, generated-code evidence, portability checks, and rejection of unsupported software semantics. |
| **Compute subsystem** | CPU, fixed-function accelerator, reconfigurable spatial array (e.g., CGRA or Reconfigurable Dataflow Architecture/RDA), or Processing-in-Memory (PIM) data-centric block; memory hierarchy (SRAM/DRAM sizing), Network-on-Chip (NoC) routing, SoC integration, interface compatibility, and relevant reliability or isolation assumptions. | Design-space comparison and rejection of candidates that only win by moving cost, bandwidth, energy, complexity, or risk elsewhere. |
| **3\ W, 3\ nm-class low-power envelope** | Power, voltage/frequency, thermal, area, EDA constraints, and dynamic power management interfaces (e.g., Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling or DVFS, power domains, thermal sensors) for the OS/firmware. | Source, version, and calibration of the power model; physical-design limits (IR drop, electromigration, timing closure); sensitivity analysis; and rejection criteria for runtime throttling or reliability failures within the scoped workload. |
| **Design-space report with evidence and rejected alternatives** | Alternatives, the Pareto frontier (the set of objective outcomes of feasible designs for which no alternative is at least as good on every objective and strictly better on at least one) [@Deb2001MultiObjective], assumptions, uncertainty, verification plan, rejected or failed candidates, and points at which the responsible architect decides whether to continue. | Measurements linked to assumptions and checks, rejected candidates, coverage, reproducible artifacts, and a named person responsible for the recommendation. |

: **What each prompt fragment requires.** The Lighthouse prompt maps to decisions about workload definition, software and ISA contracts, hardware organization, physical feasibility, and evidence. {#tbl-moonshot-decomposition tbl-colwidths="[18,34,35]"}

The table is a first-pass checklist rather than the final review form. An
answer is incomplete if it cannot identify its workload slice, software
contract, physical assumptions, supporting observations, or decision owner.
The rest of the book develops these requirements and turns them into a compact
review form.

Each row points to engineering depth that the short prompt leaves unstated. To verify whether a candidate actually fits the "3\ W, 3\ nm-class" constraint, the architect needs results from RTL, synthesis, floorplanning, timing, IR drop, leakage, thermal analysis, and final signoff. Comparing the RISC-V vector and accelerator alternatives requires checking the compiler, runtime, libraries, generated code, and software portability. Crucially, the hardest bottleneck is often the software stack. A novel spatial accelerator is dead silicon if the compiler cannot be co-adapted to target it. The Lighthouse prompt is therefore a computer architecture problem rather than a prompt engineering exercise, demanding an answer that connects decisions and evidence across the stack.

The workload and process phrases require more detail than the compact prompt provides. The XRBench suite supplies a concrete workload anchor rather than a vague application label. End-to-end XR research shows how tightly perception and display stages are coupled, making mobile XR a system-level architecture target rather than a single kernel to optimize [@HuzaifaEtAl2021ILLIXR]. AI can help here by analyzing dataset distributions to find coverage gaps, complementing profiling, trace analysis, and expert workload judgment. For instance, a model could ingest the XRBench memory trace and automatically cluster access patterns to recommend specific cache hierarchies or local scratchpads before any simulation begins.

The selected benchmark must strictly represent the system claim. Similarly, the process node is stated as a broad class rather than a named foundry process design kit (PDK)[^fn-pdk-c01]. Even though current mobile SoCs are publicly described in 3\ nm-class technology, the study must explicitly name the process, libraries, voltage assumptions, and signoff path [@Apple2024A18Pro; @Apple2024M4]. Each surviving candidate is then evaluated in a physical harness that applies PPA and static timing limits.

[^fn-pdk-c01]: **PDK (process design kit)**: The package a foundry supplies for one manufacturing process, holding the device models, standard-cell libraries, design-rule decks, and calibration data that let a tool predict whether a layout will actually work in silicon. PDKs are licensed under nondisclosure, so the physical behavior of an advanced node is largely absent from any public corpus a model could learn from.

The Lighthouse prompt fixes the workload class, 64-bit RISC-V basis, permitted
compute organizations, 3\ W envelope, 3\ nm-class low-power process, and
required design-space report. Each study must still specify the workload
version, trace, slice, and deadline; the architecture and software path; the
reference design; the process libraries and operating assumptions; and the
tools, budget, stopping rules, and checks. Those study choices may vary.
Changing the fixed conditions means answering a different challenge.

An architect might begin with an XRBench trace slice and software pipeline, propose vector-width or CPU and accelerator alternatives, and screen them with a cheap proxy. The architect can then reserve scarce compiler, simulator, RTL, or physical-design feedback for the candidates whose results could actually alter the final decision. That selection rule, along with what the resulting evidence may support, should be stated before the run.

Before any simulator runs, Amdahl's law supplies a rejection check for free. An accelerator that covers 60 percent of the XR pipeline's cycles caps whole-system speedup at 2.5 times, no matter how fast the block itself becomes [@Amdahl1967ValiditySingleProcessor]. A generated candidate whose profiled coverage cannot support its claimed system gain is ruled out by arithmetic alone, before it consumes a single simulator hour. The first question to put to a generator-proposed design is therefore not how fast the block is but how much of the workload it actually touches.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="The roofline rejects a candidate before the simulator sees it"}
**Context.** Architects own a second free screen, and this one supplies a bound rather than a ceiling. The roofline model bounds a kernel's attainable performance by its arithmetic intensity, set against the machine's peak compute and memory bandwidth [@Williams2009Roofline].

**In the XR pipeline.** One profile of the pipeline's flops per byte tells us which candidates are bandwidth-bound before a single line of RTL exists, so wider vector units on a starved kernel can be rejected on the back of an envelope. A proposal the roofline already rules out should never reach the simulator queue.
:::

Within that screening workflow, generation might produce legal vector configurations, prediction might estimate their data-movement risks, and optimization might choose which configurations merit expensive evaluation. A proxy may rank candidates one way, a simulator may overturn that ranking, and an EDA run may return timing paths and congestion rather than a single score.

This work immediately hits the cost of evaluation. Unlike a software unit test that returns a result in milliseconds, a cycle-accurate hardware simulator can take hours and physical signoff can take days. This delay makes brute-force reinforcement learning impractical and requires the study to reserve expensive checks for the candidates that merit them. Search can then overfit[^fn-overfitting-c01] a convenient fast proxy.

[^fn-overfitting-c01]: **Overfitting**: The machine-learning failure of fitting the noise of a training sample so closely that performance does not generalize to new data. An optimizer can overfit a proxy the same way, raising the measured score by exploiting the proxy's quirks rather than improving the true objective.

The longer version of the same problem is *silicon overfitting*. Because software models evolve in weeks while a design started today may ship on silicon years later, an optimizer cannot simply hyperspecialize a 3\ nm-class accelerator for today's static trace. The architect must balance specialization with enough programmability to survive the fabrication delay.

While these methods narrow the work, their output alone does not prove whether a compiler assumption holds, whether the measured behavior follows from the proposed mechanism, or whether the remaining tradeoff justifies a multimillion-dollar commitment. The final evidence should document the candidates, assumptions, measurements, and rejections that affect the claim without needing every internal model trace. The architect must resolve the remaining questions using this curated body of evidence.

A candidate is a proposed design, configuration, artifact, or measured point.
It becomes a useful result only when the measurements support a comparison
under stated conditions, the required checks were run and support the
conclusion, important alternatives and failures are recorded, and the result
can inform or close an architecture decision. Rejecting a candidate, retaining
the current architecture, or choosing a conventional method can all be useful
results.

Useful results do not need to cover the whole Lighthouse challenge. Progress
that closes one stated part without claiming an end-to-end answer is *bounded
progress*. A full-scope result addresses the complete challenge and may still
conclude that no candidate works. Full Lighthouse success requires a supported design that
meets the fixed conditions and the complete design-space report promised by the
prompt, including the software path, physical constraints, rejected
alternatives, checks, and a recommendation an independent architect can
examine.

These judgments also require two different comparisons. A reference design
shows whether one architecture is preferable to another. A credible
conventional or human-directed process shows whether AI improved the work used
to reach the result. The two comparisons are not interchangeable.

## Formulating Efficiency Claims {#sec-efficiency-claims-need-rejectable-loops}

Even if an AI-assisted process can produce a candidate and report end to end, the efficiency claim still requires a scoped system comparison. The difference between a plausible candidate and a defensible design is especially clear in an efficiency claim, because the Lighthouse subsystem cannot be judged from one score. Workload behavior, software support, data movement, physical limits, verification effort, and deployment conditions can all change which design is preferable. AI may help the architect coordinate those choices, but the resulting claim still demands evidence for the stated workload and constraints.

Efficiency is a strict claim about how well a particular architecture performs useful work with limited resources. The claim must name the exact design, workload, and resource budget it covers. A faster design fails to solve the problem if it exceeds the power budget, cannot be verified, or depends on fragile software assumptions.

Efficiency now spans far more than performance and power. Classical computer architecture made performance quantitative while treating cost and power as first-class constraints [@HennessyPatterson2017QuantitativeApproach]. Dennard-style scaling once made it easier to improve performance while keeping power density manageable [@DennardEtAl1974Scaling]. When that scaling regime weakened, dark silicon and the limits of multicore scaling pushed the field toward specialization [@BorkarChien2011FutureMicroprocessors; @EsmaeilzadehEtAl2011DarkSilicon; @HennessyPatterson2019GoldenAge].

The energy cost of data movement soon made arithmetic alone an incomplete
measure. In the cited 45\ nm data, a 32-bit integer add costs about 0.1\ pJ,
the SRAM examples range from 10 to 100\ pJ, and a DRAM access costs 1.3 to
2.6\ nJ [@Horowitz2014Energy]. These values do not determine the Lighthouse
result at a newer process node. They show why data movement can dominate and
why any accelerator that adds DRAM traffic needs an explicit system energy
comparison rather than a compute-only claim.

Warehouse-scale operation expanded the boundary to include power delivery, utilization, networking, operations, and total cost of ownership [@BarrosoHolzleRanganathan2019DatacenterAsComputer]. Today, sustainability adds operational and embodied carbon to the comparison, factors that depend heavily on energy use, hardware manufacturing, utilization, geography, and system lifetime [@GuptaEtAl2021ChasingCarbon]. An AI-assisted comparison must clearly state the assumptions and evidence relevant to each efficiency dimension and explicitly name the violations, such as DRC failures or thermal limits, that would immediately rule out a candidate during the evaluation harness review.

A valid comparison must also account for failed and rejected alternatives, not
only the winners. Keeping those results prevents later architects from
reevaluating candidates that earlier evidence ruled out. It also shows
which parts of the design space the claim actually covers.

Modern benchmark suites already reflect this broader view. MLPerf, a community
effort to make machine-learning performance claims reproducible across
systems, includes deployment scenario, latency, throughput, and accuracy in its
comparisons [@MattsonEtAl2020MLPerf]. Useful work must be evaluated
against the resource that is scarce in the stated setting, whether that is
latency, throughput, energy, power, area, cost, carbon, reliability,
verification effort, engineering time, or risk.

The design, workload, scenario, and scarce resource together define what
"efficient" means. For the Lighthouse system, a candidate that improves average
throughput may still be a poor choice if it misses an XR frame deadline, exceeds
the 3\ W envelope under sustained load, or adds verification work that the
project cannot absorb. Changing any of those conditions changes the claim and
the evidence needed to support it.

Efficiency splits along six dimensions an architect must price separately
(@tbl-efficiency-dimensions). The architect should select the dimensions that define the claim.
Reading the rows together also shows where a gain may shift cost or risk
elsewhere.

| **Dimension** | **Efficiency question** | **Why it complicates the comparison** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Performance** | How much useful work is delivered per unit time, latency budget, or service-level target? | The answer depends on workload selection, scenario, software stack, and whether the measured behavior matches the deployment claim. |
| **Power and energy** | How much useful work is delivered per watt, joule, thermal budget, or battery envelope? | A credible comparison must account for activity, data movement, voltage/frequency choices, thermal constraints, and fidelity gaps between estimates and signoff. |
| **Reliability and correctness** | How much useful work survives faults, corner cases, nondeterminism, and validation? | A faster candidate is not efficient if it spends its savings on fragility, security side-channels, debug burden, or invalid software and hardware assumptions. |
| **Scalability and cost** | How much useful work is delivered per dollar, rack, network hop, operator action, or unit of capacity? | Local wins can shift cost to memory, network, power delivery, utilization, operations, or total cost of ownership. |
| **Sustainability** | How much useful work is delivered per unit of operational and embodied environmental footprint? | Carbon depends on hardware lifetime, manufacturing, energy mix, utilization, and where and when computation runs. |
| **Evidence and engineering effort** | How much decision-relevant evidence is obtained per simulation, experiment, verification run, or engineer-hour? | Generating more candidates can still be inefficient if evaluation consumes scarce feedback, hides failures, or cannot reject weak outputs. |

: **Efficiency is six coupled dimensions, not one score:** performance, power, reliability, scalability, sustainability, and evidence cost are increasingly coupled, so a valid comparison must show when an apparent improvement shifts cost or changes the scope. {#tbl-efficiency-dimensions tbl-colwidths="[22,32,34]"}

Two kinds of efficiency operate in this comparison. The proposed hardware system must perform useful work within its resource limits, and the study itself must allocate simulator runs, physical-design experiments, verification effort, and expert review carefully enough to reach a reliable conclusion. Reducing the cost of the study is valuable only when the remaining observations can still distinguish the alternatives and expose the failures that matter to the decision.

These efficiency dimensions interact. In the mobile XR setting anchored by XRBench and ILLIXR, frame latency, energy, sustained power, and data movement are so tightly coupled that a gain in one can violate a deadline or thermal limit in another. Better simulated performance can be offset by added verification work, and lower energy may depend on fragile software assumptions. A candidate that wins under a proxy may fail on a more faithful workload. The architect must explain which tradeoffs are acceptable for the stated constraints, defining the scope of the efficiency claim instead of relying on a single attractive artifact or score.

These coupled requirements do not imply that every architecture project needs
AI. Conventional architecture methods may remain preferable when the design
question and permitted change are narrow enough to evaluate directly and the
required feedback is cheap and dependable. We should first identify what
familiar models, scripts, simulators, and expert reviews already handle well
before stating exactly what we expect AI to improve. The test is whether the
assistance leads to a better system or a more reliable conclusion, rather than
simply generating more artifacts.

A common objection is that today's models hallucinate and cannot be trusted to
produce correct hardware, so an AI-assisted architecture program is premature.
The reliability concern is valid, but no architecture method should be trusted
without checks. The practical question is whether the method and its required
checks improve the architecture result, lower the total cost of reaching a
result of comparable quality, or both, relative to competent conventional
work. If every bad proposal requires a multi-hour synthesis run, evaluation can
consume more engineering time and computation than the method saves.

The Lighthouse prompt makes this friction concrete. The requested subsystem must support a workload class, meet a strict power envelope, fit a technology assumption, interact correctly with software, and produce reviewable evidence. The final comparison must weigh energy, latency, memory traffic, programmability, verification, and deployment risk. While a single scalar objective may help an automated search navigate the space, it cannot substitute for architectural judgment.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{11\baselineskip}
```

## Evaluating Existing Systems

Applying this judgment to today's tools reveals both rapid progress and persistent gaps. This section does not survey the field, and @sec-appendix-b-ai-for-architecture-map carries the map. What follows is a curated set of flagship results, chosen because their successes and their limits are the most diagnostic of where AI-assisted architecture actually stands. Each is read the same way, by what it establishes and by the telltale limit it exposes.

Begin outside architecture, with the result that sets the frame. AlphaTensor searched the space of matrix-multiplication algorithms and found one that multiplies 4 by 4 matrices in 47 scalar multiplications, improving on the 49 of Strassen's two-level method for the first time in half a century [@FawziEtAl2022AlphaTensor]. Two qualifications travel with that number, and neither is a footnote. The record holds in modular arithmetic over the field of two elements rather than over the reals, and the standard-arithmetic improvements arrived at other matrix shapes. Much of the press coverage dropped both, which is a compact demonstration of the problem this book takes up. Every candidate decomposition admitted an exact algebraic check, and a single scalar counted the multiplications, so invalid candidates were inexpensive to discard relative to a physical design study. Complete architecture claims rarely have one check with the same scope, cost, and decisiveness. Read the rest of this section by asking how evaluation cost, fidelity, task scope, and access to evidence limit what each result establishes.

Inside architecture, tensor-program autotuning approaches that regime. Predictive design-space exploration uses simulated performance to train surrogate models that estimate behavior across a specified design space [@IpekEtAl2006PredictiveDSE]. AutoTVM uses measured hardware execution to guide a statistical search for tensor-program schedules [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM]. In each case, the input, architecture job, feedback source, and result scope remain clear. AutoTVM operates in a setting where many candidate schedules can run on real hardware quickly and most failures remain contained within the tuning run. That property makes the search practical, but it also limits what the result says about the rest of the system.

AlphaChip, a learning-based macro-placement method, is a prominent physical-design example. Its inputs are a netlist and macro descriptions, its job is macro placement, and its feedback comes from proxy rewards such as wirelength and congestion [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement]. Its reported placement speed established how fast the method produces a candidate, not that it beats strong classical baselines, and its reported deployment across several TPU generations [@GoogleDeepMind2024AlphaChip; @GoldieEtAl2024AlphaChipAddendum] is relevant evidence without settling that matched comparison. @sec-feedback-verification-trust examines the proxy-metric and baseline dispute in full.

Where the feedback is a simulator rather than silicon, the harness starts to matter more than the searcher. ArchGym placed a family of architecture simulators behind one interface and gave competing search algorithms equal sample budgets, finding that no algorithm dominates across design spaces [@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym]. That is a finding about experimental design rather than about any optimizer, and it inherits every fidelity limit of the simulators sitting behind it. Two learned design-space explorations bracket what such evidence can be made to carry. Apollo showed that transfer across related accelerator design spaces makes learned search sample-efficient in industrial practice, evaluated against fast proxies and staying inside one company's accelerator template [@yazdanbakhsh2021apollo]. BOOM-Explorer found efficient microarchitectures of an open-source RISC-V core through a real VLSI flow, where hours per sample cap the space it can afford to see [@BaiEtAl2021BOOMExplorer]. The pair is worth holding together, because the industrial result is the one an outsider cannot reproduce and the reproducible result is the one that had to buy its evidence by the hour.

Generation methods have begun to reach real hardware in narrow settings. In a conversational study, a language model drafted the Verilog for a small 8-bit processor that reached tapeout, though a human guided the model through many revisions [@BlockloveEtAl2023ChipChat]. A separate method that learns a CPU's logic from input-output examples produced a RISC-V core, Enlightenment-1, that was fabricated and runs Linux, reaching that result through a non-agentic search rather than a tool-using loop [@ChengEtAl2024AutomatedCPU]. Each reaches silicon on a narrow slice of the problem, and no autonomous loop has yet carried a full architecture study from intent to fabricated hardware. Measuring that generation ability has itself become standard practice, with VerilogEval and RTLLM scoring models on shared RTL tasks [@VerilogEval; @RTLLM], and scores have climbed fast enough that a revisit of the benchmark reports saturation and contamination pressure worth taking seriously [@PinckneyEtAl2024RevisitingVerilogEval]. What those benchmarks certify is that generated code passes a small functional testbench, which is several signoff stages short of a design.

Industrial deployment tells a different story from the academic record, and it is harder to read. Domain-adapted models trained on proprietary design data outperform much larger general models at internal assistance work such as EDA scripting, bug triage, and engineering question answering, which suggests the near-term industrial shape is an assistant beside the flow rather than an agent inside it [@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo]. A language-model agent can also plan and drive a real synthesis-to-layout tool flow from natural-language intent, though it orchestrates existing tools on small designs and its correctness rides entirely on the tools it calls [@HeEtAl2024ChatEDA]. Learned search over flow parameters has crossed into routine commercial use, with vendor-reported production tapeouts in the hundreds [@Synopsys2023DSOai]. That last claim is the one to sit with. Its evidence standard is a press release, with no public methodology, no baseline, and no matched comparison, and it is nonetheless among the most widely repeated evidence that this technology works at scale.

The pattern across all of them is easier to see side by side (@tbl-existing-systems). Reading down the limits column reveals several different constraints on the claim, including check cost and fidelity, task scope, baseline quality, workflow coverage, and whether an outside reviewer can inspect the evidence.

| **System** | **What it establishes** | **The telltale limit** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AlphaTensor [@FawziEtAl2022AlphaTensor] | Learned search can pass a fifty-year human frontier and prove the result correct | The check is exact, inexpensive, and algebraic, and one scalar scores it |
| AutoTVM [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM] | Measured search can improve schedules when many candidates run quickly on real hardware | The result covers tensor-program schedules, where failures are usually contained within the tuning run |
| AlphaChip [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement] | A learned policy produces macro placements a production flow accepts | The reward is proxy wirelength and congestion, and the matched baseline is disputed |
| ArchGym [@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym] | At equal sample budgets no search algorithm dominates, so the harness and budget shape the result | Every candidate is graded by a simulator, so the result inherits its fidelity limits |
| Apollo and BOOM-Explorer [@yazdanbakhsh2021apollo; @BaiEtAl2021BOOMExplorer] | Learned design-space exploration works in industry and through a public VLSI flow | Apollo scores fast proxies inside one firm's template; BOOM-Explorer is reproducible but pays hours per sample |
| VerilogEval and RTLLM [@VerilogEval; @RTLLM] | RTL generation is measurable on shared tasks, and scores climb fast | Passing means clearing a small testbench, with no synthesis, timing, or physical constraints |
| Chip-Chat and Enlightenment-1 [@BlockloveEtAl2023ChipChat; @ChengEtAl2024AutomatedCPU] | Generated logic has reached silicon, in one case a core that boots Linux | A human drove one and a non-agentic search the other, so no autonomous loop reached silicon |
| ChatEDA [@HeEtAl2024ChatEDA] | An agent can plan and invoke a real tool flow from stated intent | It drives existing tools on small designs, so correctness rides on the tools it calls |
| ChipNeMo [@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo] | Domain-adapted models beat far larger general models at internal design assistance | The metric is rated helpfulness on assistive tasks, and none of it is externally reproducible |
| DSO.ai [@Synopsys2023DSOai] | Learned flow-parameter search is in routine commercial use at reported production scale | The evidence standard is a press release, with no public methodology or matched baseline |

: **The strength of each result depends on its scope and how it was evaluated:** Exact, inexpensive checks support strong scoped claims, while narrow measurements, proxies, weak baselines, and supporting data, methods, or artifacts that outsiders cannot inspect each limit what an architect can conclude. {#tbl-existing-systems tbl-colwidths="[20,37,43]"}

These tools succeed at their individual tasks while exposing the integration problem that a whole architecture study must solve. Adjacent fields faced a version of it and moved forward by adopting shared baselines, standardized datasets, and common evaluation. ImageNet [@RussakovskyEtAl2015ImageNet] gave computer vision a common benchmark, and CASP (Critical Assessment of Structure Prediction) [@MoultEtAl1995CASP] let AlphaFold's [@JumperEtAl2021AlphaFold] structure predictions be measured against community-held standards. Computer architecture needs the same shared tasks, public datasets, and open evaluation protocols to turn narrow tool use into a reviewable AI-assisted practice.

Progress toward the moonshot will require more than isolated demonstrations. In software engineering, SWE-bench turns real GitHub-issue fixes into a shared task graded by automated repository tests, giving coding agents a relatively quick and repeatable task-level signal (@fig-swebench-progress) [@JimenezEtAl2024SWEBench]. Passing those tests does not prove complete software correctness, but it supports a specific claim about resolving the issue under the benchmark conditions. Hardware also has fast checks for specific properties. A complete system-and-chip claim, however, must connect functional verification with synthesis, timing, power, physical-design, and thermal evidence whose cost and fidelity differ.

```{python}
#| label: fig-swebench-progress
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Standardized task-level checks support rapid iteration on SWE-bench Verified.** Best reported SWE-bench Verified score [@JimenezEtAl2024SWEBench], one point per released model, tracked through Epoch AI's benchmarking hub [@EpochAI2025AIModels]; the line traces the best result to date. Scores climbed from roughly a third of this human-filtered 500-task subset to over four-fifths in about seventeen months. Repository tests provide a quick, repeatable signal for the defined task, while a complete architecture claim must combine functional and physical evidence from several tools.
#| out-width: "88%"
#| fig-alt: "Scatter of SWE-bench Verified resolved percentage versus model release date from late 2024 to 2026. Points climb from about 31 percent to about 84 percent, with a line tracing the best-to-date frontier through GPT-4o, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Claude Opus 4, GPT-5, and Claude Opus 4.7."

import csv
import datetime
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style
from _python.labels import place_labels

apply_style()

# Data: SWE-bench Verified results [@JimenezEtAl2024SWEBench] tracked in Epoch
# AI's benchmarking hub [@EpochAI2025AIModels]; best score per released model.
# Values dataset-transcribed. Accessed 2026-07-19.
# Receipt: data/source-receipts/chapter1-swebench-verified.csv
_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]

def _yfrac(text):
    for fmt in ("%Y-%m-%d", "%Y-%m", "%Y"):
        try:
            d = datetime.datetime.strptime(text.strip(), fmt)
            return d.year + (d.timetuple().tm_yday - 1) / 365.25
        except ValueError:
            continue
    return None

pts = []
```
