```{python}
with open(_root / "data" / "source-receipts" / "chapter1-swebench-verified.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    for row in csv.DictReader(fh):
        x = _yfrac(row["release_date"])
        try:
            score = float(row["resolved_fraction"])
        except ValueError:
            continue
        if x is None:
            continue
        pts.append({"model": row["model"], "score": score * 100 if score <= 1 else score, "x": x})
pts.sort(key=lambda p: p["x"])
best = -1.0
frontier = []
for p in pts:
    if p["score"] > best:
        best = p["score"]
        frontier.append(p)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 3.2))
ax.scatter([p["x"] for p in pts], [p["score"] for p in pts], s=16, marker="o",
           facecolors="white", edgecolors=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.7, zorder=2, label="Model releases")
ax.plot([p["x"] for p in frontier], [p["score"] for p in frontier], color=COLORS["evidence"], lw=1.6, zorder=3)
ax.scatter([p["x"] for p in frontier], [p["score"] for p in frontier], s=22, marker="o",
           facecolor=COLORS["evidence"], edgecolor=COLORS["evidence_ink"], linewidth=0.5, zorder=4, label="Best to date")
ax.set_xlim(2024.8, 2026.55)
ax.set_ylim(20, 92)
ax.set_xlabel("Model release date", fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_ylabel("SWE-bench Verified resolved (%)", fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_xticks([2025.0, 2025.5, 2026.0, 2026.5])
ax.set_xticklabels(["2025", "mid-25", "2026", "mid-26"], fontsize=6.4)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=6.4, length=2.5, width=0.6)
for _sp in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[_sp].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(True, which="major", axis="y", color=COLORS["row"], linewidth=0.4, zorder=0)
ax.legend(loc="lower right", frameon=False, fontsize=6.0, handletextpad=0.3, labelspacing=0.3)
want = ["GPT-4o", "Claude 3.7 Sonnet", "Claude Opus 4", "GPT-5", "Claude Opus 4.7"]
by_name = {}
for p in frontier:
    key = (p["model"] or "").strip()
    if key in want and key not in by_name:
        by_name[key] = p
items = [(by_name[w]["x"], by_name[w]["score"], w) for w in want if w in by_name]
place_labels(ax, fig, items, fontsize=5.0, color=COLORS["ink"])
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.10, right=0.97, top=0.98, bottom=0.12)
```

The climb shows what a standardized, automated task-level check can help enable alongside improvements in models and engineering. Best reported scores rose from roughly a third of the benchmark issues to over four-fifths in about seventeen months. Architecture also uses fast analytical, structural, and functional checks, but no single one closes a complete system-and-chip claim. Timing closure, design rules, power targets, and thermal limits require later and more expensive evidence. Fast static analysis and calibrated proxies can reduce that cost by screening candidates, but they do not replace the implementation checks on which a physical claim depends.

SPEC-style benchmarks made performance claims more comparable by specifying workloads, run rules, and reporting standards, and a benchmark that becomes standard also steers which improvements a community goes after [@Patterson2012Benchmarks]. Shared simulators such as gem5 made architecture experiments easier to inspect across labs. FPGA-accelerated simulation platforms such as FireSim, community benchmark suites such as MLPerf, artifact-evaluation practices, and open tool flows succeeded because they let researchers understand, rerun, challenge, and safely build on reported results [@SPEC2017CPU; @BinkertEtAl2011Gem5; @KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim; @MattsonEtAl2020MLPerf]. AI-assisted results will need the same shared tasks, tool interfaces, and evidence standards to matter beyond a single study.

## Data Scarcity and the Verification Load {#sec-data-scarcity-verification-load}

If these systems and tools are so promising, why is AI-assisted architecture not a solved problem? Two forces hold it back, and both trace to how little hardware design data reaches the open world and how much of the remaining work is verification. The first force has a name, *dark data*, design knowledge that exists in volume inside companies but never reaches any public corpus.

Software and hardware diverge sharply on the data axis. Public software corpora contain far more source changes, technical discussions, and tests that expose software modifications and their surrounding explanations. In contrast, high-fidelity hardware IP, process design kits (PDKs), and production silicon design data are proprietary, closely held, and rarely published. Public training corpora therefore contain far fewer examples that connect RTL and architecture choices to power-delivery routing or 3\ nm timing behavior. A generator trained largely on public text may reproduce plausible syntax without representing foundry-specific constraints, so its outputs still require constraint-aware representations and appropriate tool checks.

A method need not infer every physical constraint from training data. An architect can supply specifications and analytical models, encode formal constraints in the representation, retrieve current documentation, or use tool results to revise a candidate. Tool-guided repair after a DRC error or timing violation is one route [@TsaiEtAl2024RTLFixer], but each route exposes different information and has different costs. Open hardware ecosystems such as RISC-V and OpenROAD [@AjayiEtAl2019OpenROAD] are important public resources because they connect shareable designs to executable synthesis and physical-design flows. They complement proprietary data, domain adaptation, synthetic examples, and physics-based models rather than serving as the only route. Their smaller scale relative to public software corpora raises the value of sample-efficient methods, better representations, and explicit constraints.

Scarce data also raises the verification stakes. A model that cannot generate correct hardware zero-shot[^fn-zero-shot-c01] may emit plausible but subtly flawed structures, and industry data shows that verification consumes roughly half of total project engineering effort, with design engineers spending about half their time in verification [@Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy]. If a generator produces thousands of novel accelerators a day but engineers must manually write UVM[^fn-uvm-c01] testbenches for them, it has moved the limiting work to verification. Producing candidates faster than reviewers can check them deepens that backlog, so formal-verification tools and constrained-random testing remain part of the work rather than an afterthought. A generated cache controller that hides a coherence deadlock is worse than useless if the deadlock takes months to find. The cost of a defect can rise sharply when it escapes into later validation stages or fabricated silicon. This escalation makes early analytical, functional, formal, and physical checks economically important; @sec-feedback-verification-trust develops the multi-fidelity discipline it motivates.

[^fn-zero-shot-c01]: **Zero-shot generation**: Producing an output for a task without task-specific examples or iterative feedback. A first-pass RTL result still requires checks against the design specification and implementation constraints. Examples, retrieved knowledge, explicit constraints, domain adaptation, and tool-guided revision can all improve later attempts.

[^fn-uvm-c01]: **UVM (Universal Verification Methodology)**: The standard SystemVerilog class library teams use to build constrained-random testbenches, supplying reusable stimulus drivers, monitors, scoreboards, and coverage collectors. The testbench is often larger than the design it checks, so generating hardware faster only helps if the verification collateral scales with it.

Verification must also reach past functional correctness when the design's threat model includes hardware security. Spectre showed that functionally correct processors can still expose microarchitectural side channels [@KocherEtAl2019Spectre]. An AI-assisted study that generates security-relevant hardware must apply independent checks appropriate to the design and threat model, which may include isolation properties, side-channel analysis, or checks for malicious modifications. Generation may help produce SystemVerilog assertions, security properties, and testbenches, but it does not establish its own correctness.

Even when the data exist, a design change stated in one sentence may require
many files and long-running commands before the toolchain returns a result. The
remaining chapters take this challenge from diagnosis to decision. The study
card in @sec-architecture-20-ontology, the worked example in
@sec-running-the-loop, and the checklist in
@sec-appendix-a-reviewer-checklist give readers compact ways to apply and
review the approach.

## Open Research Questions

Every chapter in this book ends here, with the questions its argument leaves open. These sections mark where the work runs out rather than summarizing what was settled, so a reader who wants to push further knows where the edges are.

These are the widest questions the book asks, and they name blockers rather than projects. The moonshot depends on more than one capability. Across the program, studies must preserve cross-layer relationships, represent design knowledge that may be incomplete or proprietary, choose appropriate methods, use evidence at the fidelities each claim requires, and support a complete-system comparison against a credible alternative.

**When is no AI the better choice for an architecture study?** A useful answer must predict whether assistance can improve the result or lower the total cost before a team pays for data preparation, tool integration, and verification. Conventional analysis may remain better when the question and permitted change are narrow enough to evaluate directly and the required feedback is cheap and dependable.

**How can a method change one part of a design without losing the system relationships that determine its value?** Workload phases, compiler choices, memory traffic, interfaces, and physical constraints can reverse a local gain. A usable method must preserve those dependencies without making the design problem intractable.

**How can learned methods account for design knowledge that is proprietary, incomplete, or changing?** Production silicon data and foundry-calibrated behavior rarely reach public corpora, while workloads, software, libraries, and physical assumptions continue to change. The open problem includes representations, constrained methods, domain adaptation, and ways to use private or synthetic information without hiding the result's limits.

**When should prediction, generation, and optimization be used alone or in combination?** The best choice depends on the structure of the design space, the information available, the cost of obtaining a result, and the work an architect can review. No general rule yet predicts which combination will outperform a competent conventional approach.

**Which inexpensive checks can screen candidates without discarding viable designs?** Amdahl's law and the roofline expose some impossible claims before simulation, but learned proxies and simplified models can also bias which candidates survive. Research must establish both what an early check catches and which promising designs it might hide.

**How can an outside reviewer judge a complete system-and-chip claim when measurements span different tools and some design data cannot be published?** Performance, energy, reliability, software support, physical feasibility, and verification effort may come from tools with different errors and access restrictions. The comparison still needs enough independently checkable support to show what improved and where cost or risk moved.

**How can a study separate architecture quality from the contribution made by AI across a complete system-and-chip result?** Success at RTL generation, placement, scheduling, or search may leave the workload, software path, interfaces, and physical constraints unresolved. A matched comparison must connect those specific gains to result quality, total cost, starting information, tool access, and human work without reducing either judgment to one score.

**What early result should cause a long-range AI-assisted design program to change direction?** A moonshot can depend on a capability that remains plausible without becoming useful. Programs need results that expose when the expected architecture benefit or cost reduction is not arriving while there is still time to revise the premise.

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="A candidate is not yet an architecture result"}
Automation can propose candidates, but the architect still defines the
comparison, conditions, and checks required before a candidate supports an
architecture conclusion.
:::


The Lighthouse prompt is the moonshot this chapter proposes, and it is a target
rather than a result. It fixes a system-and-chip challenge across workload,
software, hardware, physical constraints, verification, and the final
recommendation. Each study must supply the exact conditions needed to test its
part of that challenge. A candidate becomes a useful result only when its
measurements and checks support an architecture decision. A useful result can
close a stated part of the challenge and justify the next study without being
mistaken for full Lighthouse success.

Amdahl's law and the roofline show why architecture reasoning should precede
expensive tool work. The first tests whether the proposed change covers enough
of the workload to support the claimed system gain. The second tests whether
the machine can supply enough data to use the proposed compute. A candidate
that fails either bound should not consume simulator or physical-design time.

The same discipline applies after a candidate survives. A full Lighthouse result
must account for performance, energy, power delivery, reliability, cost,
verification effort, and the time needed to reach a defensible conclusion. A
gain in one dimension can still lose the comparison by shifting cost or risk
into another.

Three judgments remain separate. The architecture outcome states which design,
if any, the measurements support. The AI contribution states whether assistance
improved that result, lowered the total cost of reaching a result of comparable
quality, or both, relative to a credible conventional or human-directed
process. The program status states whether repeated comparisons support the
Architecture 2.0 bet. Under matched conditions, the bet has failed within the
assessed program if AI improves neither the architecture result nor the total
cost of reaching a defensible decision. The public evidence reviewed for this
edition leaves that verdict open, and @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect
develops the comparison needed to judge it.

Current systems should therefore be read by the architecture work they address,
the cost and fidelity of their evaluation, and what their results can establish.
Exact, inexpensive checks can support strong scoped search claims, while slow
simulators, imperfect proxies, narrow task scope, and supporting material that
outsiders cannot inspect limit the conclusion. The architect still frames the task,
chooses the abstractions and tools, interprets the result, and remains
answerable for the committed design.

The fixed Lighthouse challenge, useful-result standard, and open program test
now lead to a different question. Specialization, software change, evaluation
cost, and cross-layer coordination can make a real architecture comparison
difficult to finish. @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales turns those pressures
into a diagnosis of the work preventing a decision.
